topics.title: Strings compare lexicographically
topics.body: `<` compares character by character, so `apple` sorts before `banana` and the comparison is stable across platforms.

topics.title: append grows a string in place
topics.body: `append` adds characters to the existing string instead of creating a third one, which keeps the capacity it already has.

topics.title: erase removes a range of characters
topics.body: `erase(pos, count)` deletes from the middle and shifts the rest left, shrinking the string.

topics.title: length and size report the same count
topics.body: Both return the number of characters; `size` exists so strings share an interface with the other containers.

topics.title: find returns npos when nothing matches
topics.body: A search compares against `std::string::npos`; testing against anything else can silently succeed.

topics.title: A pointer can be reassigned
topics.body: Unlike a reference, a pointer is an object holding an address, so it can point at one variable and later at another.

topics.title: const can qualify the pointer or the pointee
topics.body: `const int*` forbids writing through the pointer, while `int* const` forbids changing where it points.

topics.title: nullptr compares equal to itself
topics.body: A null pointer is falsy, so `if (p)` is the concise check before dereferencing.

topics.title: make_unique constructs in place
topics.body: It allocates and forwards the arguments to the constructor in one expression, so no raw pointer ever exists to leak.

topics.title: unique_ptr cannot be copied
topics.body: Copying would create two owners, so the copy constructor is deleted; only `std::move` transfers ownership.

topics.title: shared_ptr resets its count
topics.body: `reset` drops one owner; when the count reaches zero the object is destroyed and its memory returned.

topics.title: RAII frees at the end of the scope
topics.body: The destructor runs when the owning object leaves its block, which is why no explicit cleanup is needed.

topics.title: new[] needs delete[]
topics.body: Array allocation and array deletion are different functions; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

topics.title: A namespace avoids a name clash
topics.body: Two functions with the same name can coexist in different namespaces, and the caller chooses with the scope operator.

topics.title: using brings one name into scope
topics.body: A using-declaration imports a single name, which is narrower than a using-directive and easier to reason about.

topics.title: Aggregate initialization fills fields in order
topics.body: Braced initialization assigns members in declaration order, so a missing value becomes zero.

topics.title: A union shares one storage
topics.body: All members of a union start at the same address, so writing one overwrites the others; the size is the largest member.

topics.title: typedef and using name the same type
topics.body: Both create an alias; `using` reads left to right and works with templates, which is why new code prefers it.

topics.title: this points at the current object
topics.body: Inside a member function `this` is the address of the object the call was made on, which is how chaining returns itself.

topics.title: Encapsulation hides the representation
topics.body: Callers see methods, not fields, so the internal type can change without breaking them.

topics.title: Objects can be copied
topics.body: The compiler-generated copy constructor copies each member, which is enough when the members manage themselves.

topics.title: Static members belong to the class
topics.body: A static data member is shared by every object, and a static function can be called without an instance.

topics.title: A class can hold another class
topics.body: Containment lets one type reuse another without inheritance, and the contained object is constructed automatically.

topics.title: A constructor runs once per object
topics.body: Every object is constructed exactly once, and the constructor’s body is the first code that sees a fully allocated object.

topics.title: Destruction is the reverse of construction
topics.body: Locals are destroyed in reverse order of construction, which is why later objects can still rely on earlier ones.

topics.title: Copy assignment returns the object
topics.body: Returning `*this` lets `a = b = c` chain, and the parameter is a const reference to avoid a copy.

topics.title: explicit blocks an implicit conversion
topics.body: Marking a one-argument constructor `explicit` stops the compiler from turning an int into the class behind your back.

topics.title: A delegating constructor shares the work
topics.body: One constructor can call another, so validation lives in a single place instead of being copied.

topics.title: is-a and has-a are different questions
topics.body: Inheritance answers "is a kind of"; composition answers "contains". Choosing the wrong one makes later changes expensive.

topics.title: protected reaches derived classes
topics.body: A protected member is invisible to unrelated code but available to a derived class, which is the middle ground between public and private.

topics.title: Construction runs base then derived
topics.body: The base subobject must exist before the derived body can use it, so its constructor completes first.

topics.title: Destruction runs derived then base
topics.body: The derived part is destroyed first because it may depend on the base, and the base is torn down last.

topics.title: Composition keeps the parts independent
topics.body: A containing class can swap the contained type without changing its own interface, which inheritance cannot do.
